title: Convert BTU to kcal (Air Conditioning): Calculator + Table | Hacé Cuentas
h1: BTU to kcal Converter for Air Conditioning
description: Convert BTU/hr to kcal/hr instantly. 1 BTU = 0.251996 kcal. Free calculator + reference table for sizing AC units — works both ways.
answerSnippet: 1 BTU = 0.251996 kcal (kilocalories). To convert BTU/hr to kcal/hr, multiply by 0.251996. For example, a 12,000 BTU/hr air conditioner equals 3,023.95 kcal/hr. To go the other way, multiply kcal by 3.96832 to get BTU.
intro:
This calculator converts between **BTU/hr** (British Thermal Units per hour) and **kcal/hr** (kilocalories per hour) — the two most common ratings for air conditioning capacity. The exact conversion factor is **1 BTU = 0.251996 kcal** (or 1 kcal = 3.96832 BTU), based on the International Table calorie defined by NIST.

US-market AC units are always rated in BTU/hr, while many Asian and European models use kcal/hr. Knowing the conversion lets you compare specs across brands and countries, size a room unit correctly, and read energy labels from different markets.
keyTakeaway: **1 BTU = 0.251996 kcal — a 12,000 BTU/hr window unit delivers exactly 3,023.95 kcal/hr of cooling. A 3,500 kcal/hr imported mini-split equals 13,889 BTU/hr.**
useCases: Comparing a US-spec 18,000 BTU/hr central AC unit against a European model rated in kcal/hr to confirm equivalent cooling power before purchase.
Calculating whether a 9,000 BTU/hr portable air conditioner (≈2,268 kcal/hr) is sufficient to cool a 350 sq ft bedroom in a hot climate.
Converting manufacturer datasheets from kcal/hr to BTU/hr when importing HVAC equipment from Japan, China, or Europe for installation in a US building.
Sizing a supplemental window unit for a home office: verifying that a 6,000 BTU/hr unit (~1,512 kcal/hr) meets the ASHRAE rule-of-thumb of 20 BTU per sq ft for a 300 sq ft space.
explanation:
## How the Conversion Works

The conversion between BTU and kcal is fixed by thermodynamic definitions — these are both units of heat energy:

```
BTU → kcal:   kcal = BTU × 0.251996
kcal → BTU:   BTU  = kcal × 3.96832

For capacity ratings (per hour):
  kcal/hr = (BTU/hr) × 0.251996
  BTU/hr  = (kcal/hr) × 3.96832

Example — 12,000 BTU/hr window unit:
  12,000 × 0.251996 = 3,023.95 kcal/hr

Example — 3,500 kcal/hr imported mini-split:
  3,500 × 3.96832 = 13,888.9 BTU/hr
```

The factor 0.251996 comes from the International Table (IT) calorie. NIST defines 1 BTU (IT) = 1,055.05585 joules and 1 kcal (IT) = 4,186.8 joules, giving the ratio 1,055.05585 ÷ 4,186.8 = **0.251996**.

---

## Practical Examples

**Buying an imported mini-split:**
A Japanese unit is rated at 2,800 kcal/hr.
2,800 × 3.96832 = **11,111 BTU/hr** — close to a 1-ton unit. You'd look for a 12,000 BTU/hr equivalent in US catalogs.

**Sizing a home office (200 sq ft):**
ASHRAE guideline: ~20 BTU/sq ft for 8-ft ceilings in moderate climates.
200 × 20 = 4,000 BTU/hr → 4,000 × 0.251996 = **1,008 kcal/hr**. A 5,000 BTU/hr unit (1,260 kcal/hr) gives a comfortable safety margin.

**Multi-zone system total:**
12,000 + 9,000 + 6,000 BTU/hr = 27,000 BTU/hr
27,000 × 0.251996 = **6,803.9 kcal/hr** — useful when specifying a chiller rated in kcal/hr by a European manufacturer.

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Confusing BTU with BTU/hr:** BTU is energy; BTU/hr is power (cooling capacity). AC units are rated in BTU/hr. The conversion factor is the same for both, but don't apply a BTU-energy value to an hourly capacity.

2. **Using the wrong calorie type:** Thermochemical calorie = 4,184 J; IT calorie = 4,186.8 J. For HVAC, always use the **IT calorie** (factor 0.251996). The thermochemical factor (0.252164) introduces ~0.07% error.

3. **Ignoring EER/COP:** BTU/hr describes *capacity*, not *efficiency*. Two 12,000 BTU/hr units can consume very different amounts of electricity depending on their EER or SEER rating.

faq.q: What is the exact BTU to kcal conversion factor?
faq.a: **1 BTU = 0.251996 kcal** (International Table calorie). The inverse is 1 kcal = 3.96832 BTU. This is based on NIST definitions: 1 BTU (IT) = 1,055.05585 joules and 1 kcal (IT) = 4,186.8 joules, giving the ratio 1,055.05585 ÷ 4,186.8 = 0.251996.

faq.q: How many kcal/hr is a 12,000 BTU/hr air conditioner?
faq.a: A 12,000 BTU/hr unit (1-ton AC) = **3,023.95 kcal/hr**. Calculation: 12,000 × 0.251996 = 3,023.95. This is why many Asian-market ACs advertised as '3,000 kcal/hr' correspond closely to a 1-ton US unit.
3,500 kcal/hr × 3.96832 = **13,888.9 BTU/hr** — slightly above a 1-ton unit and below a 1.5-ton. This is a common rating for medium-sized imported mini-splits from Japan, Korea, or China.

faq.q: Why do some AC units show kcal/hr instead of BTU/hr?
faq.a: Japan, China, South Korea, and much of Europe historically rated HVAC equipment in kcal/hr. The US and UK standardized on BTU/hr. Today the SI unit is kW, but BTU/hr dominates US retail. When comparing or importing international equipment, you need to convert kcal/hr to BTU/hr (or vice versa).

faq.q: Is converting BTU/hr to kcal/hr the same as converting BTU to kcal?
faq.a: Yes — the 'per hour' cancels algebraically, so the factor is identical: multiply BTU/hr by **0.251996** to get kcal/hr. Just don't mix up a single BTU (energy quantity) with a BTU/hr (power or capacity rating) from an AC nameplate.

faq.q: What is 1 kW in BTU/hr and kcal/hr?
faq.a: **1 kW = 3,412.14 BTU/hr = 859.85 kcal/hr**. So a 3.5 kW mini-split = 11,942 BTU/hr ≈ 3,007 kcal/hr — just under a 1-ton unit. European heat pumps rated in kW can be converted using these factors.

faq.q: How do I size an AC unit for my room using BTU/hr?
faq.a: The ASHRAE rule of thumb is approximately **20 BTU/hr per square foot** of floor area for standard 8-ft ceilings. A 300 sq ft room needs ~6,000 BTU/hr (≈1,512 kcal/hr). Add 10% for south-facing or very sunny rooms, and ~600 BTU/hr per extra occupant beyond two. For precise sizing, use a Manual J load calculation.

faq.q: What does '1 ton of refrigeration' mean in kcal/hr?
faq.a: **1 ton of refrigeration = 12,000 BTU/hr = 3,023.95 kcal/hr**. It represents the cooling power needed to melt one short ton (2,000 lb) of ice in 24 hours. This is why central AC systems are commonly described as '2-ton' (24,000 BTU/hr) or '3-ton' (36,000 BTU/hr) units.

faq.q: Can I use this to compare a BTU/hr AC with a kW-rated heat pump?
faq.a: Yes. Convert: BTU/hr ÷ 3,412.14 = kW (cooling capacity). For example, 24,000 BTU/hr ÷ 3,412.14 = **7.03 kW**. Note this is cooling *capacity*, not electrical consumption — a 7 kW capacity heat pump might only draw 2 kW of electrical input if its COP is 3.5.
